lines: All of this ran purely on proof, no numbers involved. Now a different kind of choice, about a very ordinary piece of syntax.
A with clause gives a name to a query. Look at the two boxes on the right: the engine can let the rest of the query see inside it, or compute it once and pass up a sealed result.
Neither is always better, and the right answer depends on how the name is used.
Begin with how it used to work. Before version twelve of PostgreSQL, every named query was sealed, however simple.
Watch the red bar go up. The filter on the left cannot get past it, so the index on key is out of reach.
The engine scanned the whole table, copied it, and only then filtered. A one line query could cost a full scan.
That sealed box has a name: an optimization fence.
Since version twelve the default is smarter. Look at the three ticks.
A named query is inlined if it has no side effects, is not recursive, and is used exactly once.
Then the filter slides through and the index is used. The fence is gone, because there was no reason for it.
Use it twice, though, and the default flips back to computing it once.
Here are two queries over the same big table with an index on key. In one, the named query is used once, in the other twice, in a self join.
Think about which of them can pass the filter inside.
Which one uses the index by default?
answer: The self join refers to the name twice, so by default it is computed once as a temporary copy with no index. Both sides of the join read that copy.
Both using it would be true only with an override, and neither is not the case for the single use. Next, the override.

lines: You can force the inline with not materialized. Watch both references light up.
Now the filter reaches the table through each reference, and the index is used twice.
But there is a price. The base table is read once per reference, instead of once in total.
It wins when each use needs only a small slice, and loses when each one needs the lot.
The opposite case matters just as much. Suppose the named query calls an expensive function.
Compare the two rows. Materialized runs the function once for each base row. The other recomputes it for every reference.
Used twice, that is double the work, and for a volatile function it can be a different answer.
So write materialized when once is the point. A later edit that changes the number of references cannot then silently undo it.
Make it concrete. A named query calls an expensive function for each row, and it is referenced twice.
You mark it not materialized, to get the index.
How many times does the function run for each base row?
answer: Each reference is inlined and evaluates the function itself. That is the duplicated computation the documentation warns about.
It is not once, because the single evaluation was exactly what materialization gave you. And the index does not decide it.

lines: Not every engine offers the choice. SQL Server does not materialize a named query at all.
Look at the two red boxes: every reference runs the definition again.
There is no keyword to reach for. The documented answer is to compute the result once into a temporary object and refer to that.
It is the same fix as the materialized hint, done by hand.
So when do you want the fence? Three cases.
When repeating the work would duplicate something expensive. When a side effect means once is a correctness requirement. And when a separate, named step simply reads better.
Remove it when letting the optimizer reach inside saves more than the repeated work costs.
The point is that it is a trade, and you can choose it on purpose.
To sum up. Find out which behaviour your engine and version give you, because the default changed in version twelve.
State the hint explicitly where the choice matters, since a later edit can change the reference count and flip the default.
And test single evaluation with a real count, not just by reading the plan.
Whether to look inside a query is settled. Next: the numbers the optimizer leans on to choose, and how it estimates them.
Two checks. First, the release from which a once used, side effect free named query is inlined by default.
Which version?
answer: Before that, every named query was a fence, which is why code written for older versions may rely on behaviour that no longer holds.

lines: Second check. On SQL Server, a named query is referenced twice.
How many times does it execute?
answer: It re runs for each reference, and there is no materialization switch. A temporary table is the way to compute it once.
